title: Pools in production: names, errors, context, shutdown
goal: By the end you can set up a pool you can debug on its worst night: named threads, every failure reported with its request id, context carried to the worker, the right numbers on a dashboard, a clean shutdown, and no task waiting on another task in the same pool.
opening:
Picture the kitchen on a Saturday night, when the orders stop coming out. Which cook is stuck? Every cook wears the same white jacket and no name tag. Which table was the burned dish for? The note with the table number stayed with the waiter. How long has the rail been this full? Nobody kept count. And at closing time, someone turns off the lights with two dishes still in the oven.

A thread pool, the team of threads that runs a program's tasks, meets the same questions, and its defaults answer none of them. Its threads are called `pool-3-thread-7`. A task sent with `submit` can fail without a word. The request's label stays on the thread that started the work. And `shutdown()` waits for nothing. None of this shows up in a test.

The last lesson split arithmetic among cooks who steal from each other, and this one runs pools for real. In this lesson, we'll add name tags, catch every failure, carry each request's note along, read the numbers that warn of trouble, untangle a pool that waits for itself, and close the kitchen in order. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: At closing time, a job prints the day's bill for every table, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Each table's task submits a fetch of that table's orders to the same pool and calls `get()` on it. With the 5 tables of a test, it takes 2 seconds. On a busy Saturday there are 400 tables. What happens?
options: It takes about 80 times longer, because the pool is busy
The pool grows past 20 threads to keep up
It hangs forever, with the CPU near zero
The JVM detects the deadlock and throws in one of the tasks
warmup.why: The first 20 bill tasks take every thread, and each one waits for a fetch that is queued behind 380 other bill tasks. No thread will ever be free to run a fetch, so the job hangs. A fixed pool never grows, and the JVM's deadlock detector looks for threads holding locks in a circle, not for tasks waiting on queued tasks, so nothing throws. The fourth section takes it apart.

sections.h: Name tags and lost failures: naming threads, and catching what submit hides
sections.body:
A thread's name, its name tag, shows up in log lines, in profilers (tools that show where a program spends its time) and in thread dumps. A **thread dump** is a snapshot of every thread in a running JVM, the Java Virtual Machine that runs your program, with its name, its state and the line of code it is on. You can take one with `jcmd <pid> Thread.print`, where `<pid>` is the number the operating system gave the program.

The ready-made pools from `Executors` name their threads `pool-3-thread-7`, the seventh thread of the third pool. In a dump of a program with eight pools, that tells you nothing. A **thread factory** is the object a pool asks for each new thread. Hand the pool one that names its threads:

```java
ThreadFactory named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory();   // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ...
ExecutorService grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named);
```

```kotlin
val named = Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory()            // JDK 21+: grill-0, grill-1, ...
val grill = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4, named)
```

Before JDK 21 (version 21 of Java's development kit), you write a small `ThreadFactory` of your own.

Now failures. The first lesson of this track showed that `execute` and `submit` treat a failing task in opposite ways. In production, that difference decides whether you ever hear about it.

`FailureDemo`, in the Try it below, makes a pool with one thread. The factory names it `grill-0` and gives it an **`UncaughtExceptionHandler`**, the method the JVM calls when an exception escapes a thread. This one prints a line. Then it sends one failing task through each method. Predict what each half prints:

```text
1. execute() a task that throws
  handler: grill-0 died of java.lang.IllegalStateException: the grill went out
   the next task runs on grill-1
2. submit() a task that throws
   (nothing printed) the next task runs on grill-1
   only get() shows it: java.lang.IllegalStateException: a negative price
```

With `execute`, the exception escaped the task. The worker `grill-0` died, the handler ran, and the pool started `grill-1` in its place. With `submit`, the `FutureTask`, the wrapper that `submit` puts around a task, caught the exception and kept it. Nothing printed, and `grill-1` carried on. The grill going out at least made some noise. The negative price would have stayed quiet forever if the demo hadn't called `get()`. In fire-and-forget code, which hands over a task and never looks at its result, nobody does.

The default handler prints a stack trace to `System.err`, outside your logs and with no request id. So a handler on the thread factory covers only half the cases, and that half badly.

To cover both, catch failures in one place that every task passes through. `submit`, `invokeAll` and `CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(task, pool)` all end up calling `execute`. So a `ThreadPoolExecutor` subclass that overrides `execute` and wraps each task sees all of them.

The wrapper runs the task inside a `try`. A task from `execute` throws, and the `catch` reports it. A task from `submit` doesn't throw: it's a `FutureTask`, and after it runs, `state()` says `FAILED` and `exceptionNow()` (both JDK 19) hands over the original exception. Report it with the request id, and don't rethrow. Rethrowing only kills the worker and prints the same stack trace a second time. The lab builds exactly that pool, `ProductionPool`.

**`submit` hides failures and `execute` kills workers. Report both from one wrapper.**

That wrapper reports a request id, which raises a fair question: whose request id does a pool thread have?

aside.title: What is an MDC, and why do log lines need it?
aside.body: If your program logs with SLF4J, a widely used logging library for Java, it has an MDC, short for Mapped Diagnostic Context. The MDC is a small map of values for the current thread, such as the request id, and the log format can print a value from it on every line. It is built on a `ThreadLocal`, so everything in this section applies to it. Frameworks for web services often put the request id into the MDC when a request arrives, on the thread that handles it. The lab's `RequestContext` is a one-value stand-in for it.

sections.h: The board by the pass: four numbers that show a pool falling behind
sections.body:
A pool is a queue in front of a few threads, and it's often the first place a slow service shows up. A good kitchen keeps a board by the pass, and four numbers on a pool's board tell you most of what you need.

The queue size, `getQueue().size()`, is the number of tickets on the rail. A queue that keeps growing means tasks arrive faster than they finish. Little's law, from Sizing a pool (tasks inside = arrival rate x time each one stays), says each task's wait grows with it.

The active count, `getActiveCount()`, compared with the maximum, says how many cooks are busy. A pool stuck at its maximum for minutes has no room left, and it's usually waiting on something further along the path, not working hard.

The rejections are the tasks the pool turned away. `ThreadPoolExecutor` doesn't count them for you. Wrap the `RejectedExecutionHandler`, the code a pool calls when it refuses a task (Inside ThreadPoolExecutor), in one that adds to a counter and then throws.

The time in queue is how long each task waited for a thread. The caller feels that wait, and the task never measures it. Record the time when a task is submitted, in the same wrapper that carries the context, and compare it when the task starts.

`MetricsDemo` sends a burst of 10 tasks of 300 ms each to a pool of 2 threads, named `orders-`, with a queue of 4 and a counting handler. Then it prints the board every 200 ms. Predict the first row before you read it:

```text
  ms  threads  active  queued  done  rejected
   0        2       2       4     0         4
 244        2       2       4     0         4
 446        2       2       2     2         4
 647        2       2       0     4         4
 849        2       2       0     4         4
1050        2       0       0     6         4
```

Two tasks run, four wait in the queue, and four are rejected at once, since 2 + 4 = 6 is all the pool can hold. After that, every 300 ms two more finish. The queue goes 4, 2, 0, `done` climbs 0, 2, 4, 6, and `active` drops to 0 at about 900 ms. The rejected count stays at 4, and those four callers heard the bad news at once instead of waiting for it.

Picture the same burst on `newFixedThreadPool(2)`, whose queue has no limit. The board would show `rejected 0` and a queue of 8. Every task is accepted, and the last two wait 1.2 seconds before a thread even picks them up. Only the time in queue would show the trouble. That's why it belongs on the board.

The getters are approximate, as their Javadoc, the official documentation, says, because the threads change the numbers while you read them. That's fine for a dashboard and wrong for program logic. If your program already sends numbers to a dashboard, a metrics library such as Micrometer can read most of these from a pool for you.

Of the four, time in queue and rejections are what your customers feel. A pool with an empty queue and no rejections is healthy, however busy its threads look.

**Watch the queue, not just the threads. Count every rejection.**

Now picture a board where every number has frozen: all threads active, the queue full and not moving, nothing done, and the CPU idle.

sections.h: Cooks waiting for tickets behind them: pool-induced deadlock
sections.body:
At closing time, a job prints the day's bill for every table. For each table, a task fetches the table's order lines from the order book, a database, and then renders the bill. Someone split the fetch into a task of its own, on the same pool:

```java
pool.submit(() -> {
    Future<List<String>> lines = pool.submit(() -> orders.lines(table));   // a task inside a task
    return render(table, lines.get());                                     // waits for it
});
```

```kotlin
pool.submit<String> {
    val lines = pool.submit<List<String>> { orders.lines(table) }   // a task inside a task
    render(table, lines.get())                                     // waits for it
}
```

With 20 threads and the 5 tables of a test, it's fine. On a busy Saturday there are 400 tables. Let's trace it with those numbers.

1. The first 20 bill tasks take all 20 threads.
2. Each one submits its fetch, and the 20 fetches join the back of the queue, behind 380 waiting bill tasks.
3. Each bill task then waits in `get()` for its fetch.

Every thread now waits for a task that can only run on a free thread, and no thread will ever be free. In the kitchen, every cook has taken a bill ticket, pinned a "fetch the orders" ticket at the back of the rail, and stands waiting for it. No cook is left to take the fetch tickets.

`DeadlockDemo` builds the smallest case: two bill tasks on a pool of two threads named `bills-`, where each fetch takes microseconds:

```text
after 300 ms: active=2, queued=2, completed=0
no bill after 2 s: both threads wait for fetches that can never start
```

Both threads are active, the two fetches are queued, and nothing has completed. Speed isn't the problem. The demo gives up after 2 seconds, but the pool would wait forever. This is **pool-induced deadlock**, which *Java Concurrency in Practice* calls thread starvation deadlock: every thread in a bounded pool, one with a fixed number of threads, waits for a task that is queued in that same pool.

Unlike the lock deadlock of Deadlock, livelock and starvation, the CPU drops to zero, nothing throws, and a thread dump has no "deadlock found" line, because no lock is involved: every thread is simply `WAITING` in `FutureTask.get`. The figure shows the moment.

Here are three fixes, in the order I'd try them:

1. Don't block inside the pool. Compose: `supplyAsync(() -> orders.lines(t), pool).thenApply(lines -> render(t, lines))`. The render step runs as a callback, code that runs when the fetch completes, so no thread waits. Only the caller joins at the end. The demo's `fixed` mode does this and prints both bills at once, on the same two threads.
2. Don't split what doesn't need splitting. If the bill task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline, in the same task.
3. Give each stage its own pool. Bill tasks may wait for a separate fetch pool, as long as fetch tasks never wait for the bill pool. That's a bulkhead from Sizing a pool, a separate limit for each stage.

A cached pool, with no limit on threads, hides the hang by starting a thread for every waiting task, which moves the problem to memory and to the database. Calling `join()` inside a `CompletableFuture` stage is the same bug, which is why CompletableFuture: composing async steps warned against it.

**No task may wait for another task in its own bounded pool. Compose, inline, or use a second pool.**

Our pools can now run well all day. At night, they have to stop.

sections.h: Closing the kitchen at night: shutting pools down in order, within one deadline

compare.title: Carrying the MDC: an executor wrapper vs a coroutine context element

java.title: MdcExecutor.java (SLF4J)

kotlin.title: MdcCoroutine.kt (kotlinx-coroutines-slf4j)

compare.note: The Java wrapper installs the context once, because a task stays on one thread from start to finish. A coroutine, Kotlin's own light task, can move to another thread every time it suspends, so a wrapper around the whole coroutine wouldn't be enough. `MDCContext()` and `asContextElement` are thread context elements: the dispatcher installs the value each time the coroutine resumes on a thread, and restores the thread's old value when it suspends. One trap: an `MDC.put` inside the coroutine is lost at the next suspension, because the element keeps reinstalling the map it captured. The kotlinx docs say to wrap the change in `withContext(MDCContext())`.

worked.title: Diagnose a bill job that stopped on a busy Saturday

steps.say: The closing-time bill job has printed nothing for 30 minutes, and the CPU is near zero. A thread dump (`jcmd <pid> Thread.print`) shows all 20 `bills-` threads at the same spot. Before reading on, say what they are waiting for.
steps.code:
"bills-3" #41 prio=5 os_prio=0 ... waiting on condition
   java.lang.Thread.State: WAITING (parking)
	at jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.park(Native Method)
	- parking to wait for <0x...> (a java.util.concurrent.FutureTask)
	at java.util.concurrent.locks.LockSupport.park(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.awaitDone(...)
	at java.util.concurrent.FutureTask.get(...)
	at com.example.restaurant.BillJob.lambda$run$0(BillJob.java)
	...

steps.say: Every thread is inside a bill task, parked in `FutureTask.get()`, waiting for another task's result. The pool's board finishes the story: `active=20`, the queue at 380 and not moving, `completed` flat. The fetch tasks they wait for are in that queue, behind the other bill tasks, and they need a free thread that will never come. The dump has no "Found one Java-level deadlock" line, because the detector looks for threads holding locks in a circle, and a `Future` has no owner.
The fix is to stop holding a thread while waiting. Compose the fetch and the render, start every table's pipeline, and let only the job's own thread wait at the end.
steps.code:
List<CompletableFuture<String>> bills = tables.stream()
        .map(t -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> orders.lines(t), pool)   // 1. fetch on the pool
                .thenApply(lines -> render(t, lines)))                       // 2. render as a callback
        .toList();
return bills.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList();                // 3. only the caller waits
steps.alt_code:
val bills = tables.map { t ->
    CompletableFuture.supplyAsync({ orders.lines(t) }, pool)                // 1. fetch on the pool
        .thenApply { lines -> render(t, lines) }                           // 2. render as a callback
}
return bills.map { it.join() }                                             // 3. only the caller waits

steps.say: Then make the next bad night shorter. The `bills-` name tags already paid off: they showed at once which pool was stuck. Add the queue size and the oldest task's wait for this pool to the dashboard, with an alert, so a queue that stops moving wakes someone up within minutes.

lab.title: A production pool, and a bill job to untangle
steps: Meet the classes. `ProductionPool` is a `ThreadPoolExecutor` with a bounded queue, and you'll give it named threads, carried context and failure reports. `RequestContext` holds the current thread's request id in a `ThreadLocal`. `FailureLog` is where the pool reports a failed task. `BillJob` prints a bill for each table, and it hangs. Run the tests: all eight fail, and the two `BillJob` tests time out after 5 seconds. That is the deadlock.
Write `ProductionPool.create`: build the factory with `Thread.ofPlatform().name(name + "-", 0).factory()` and pass it to the private constructor, which already sets up the bounded queue.

Write `ProductionPool.execute`. Read `RequestContext.get()` first, on the calling thread. Then call `super.execute` with a lambda that saves the worker's own context, sets the captured id, runs the task, and restores the saved context in a `finally`.

Report failures inside that lambda: catch `RuntimeException | Error` from `task.run()` and report it without rethrowing. After `run()` returns, if the task is a `Future` whose `state()` is `FAILED`, report `exceptionNow()`.
Fix `BillJob.run`: start a `supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render)` pipeline for every table, then join them all on the calling thread.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: Capture the id before `super.execute`. Inside the lambda you are already on the worker, where `RequestContext.get()` returns the worker's value.
`task instanceof Future<?> f && f.state() == Future.State.FAILED` (JDK 19+), then `f.exceptionNow()`, gives you the original exception, not an `ExecutionException`.
If `reportsExecuteFailures` sees the next task on `orders-1`, your wrapper rethrew: the worker died, and the pool replaced it.
The `BillJob` fix needs no second pool. A `thenApply` callback never holds a thread while it waits.

drill.title: A context-carrying executor from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write `Executor withRequestId(Executor delegate)`: every task runs with the `RequestContext` of the thread that called `execute`, and the worker's own value is restored afterwards. Then compare. Where did you read the context, and is the restore in a `finally`?

answer.title: Contexts.java

alt.title: Contexts.kt

recap: Name every pool's threads (`Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory()` on JDK 21+), so dumps and logs say which pool is stuck.
An `UncaughtExceptionHandler` only sees `execute` failures, and `submit` hides them in the `Future`. Wrap `execute` once to report both, with the request id.
`ThreadLocal` context such as a request id doesn't follow a task to a pool. Capture it at submission, install it in the worker, and restore it in `finally`.
Watch the queue size, the active count against the maximum, rejections and time in queue. Count rejections yourself, in the handler.

A task that blocks on another task in the same bounded pool can hang the pool forever. Compose instead, do the work inline, or give each stage its own pool. Shut down in order: intake first, then pools upstream first, within one deadline.
The limit: every pool here holds one costly platform thread for each waiting task, so the thread count caps how many requests can wait at once.
closing:
We started with a stuck kitchen and questions nobody could answer. Now each has an answer: name tags on every thread, one wrapper that reports every failure with its request id, a note that travels with the order, four numbers on the board, no cook waiting for a ticket behind him, and a closing routine that fits the deadline.

Now find where your own code creates pools, and give each one a named thread factory. Then search for `.get()` and `.join()` inside tasks, and check that none waits on its own pool.

Next, we'll start the virtual threads track with the thread-per-request wall. If every waiting request holds a costly platform thread, what happens when the requests outnumber the threads?

quiz.q: A report job uses a fixed pool of 4. Each report task submits two smaller queries to the same pool and calls `get()` on both. It passes every test, then hangs on the busiest day with the CPU near zero. What happened?
options: The queries got slow, so the reports need more time
Four report tasks hold all four threads, and each waits for queries queued behind other reports, so nothing can ever finish
Two report tasks locked each other's monitors
The queue overflowed, and the queries were rejected
quiz.why: This is pool-induced deadlock. The awaited tasks need a free thread, and all the threads are busy waiting for them. Slowness wouldn't keep the CPU at zero forever, no monitors are involved, and a fixed pool's queue has no limit, so nothing is rejected.

quiz.q: A request thread puts `req-42` in a `ThreadLocal` (such as a logging library's MDC) and submits a task to a fixed pool. The task logs a line. With no context propagation in place, which request id is on that line?
options: `req-42`, because pool threads inherit the submitter's ThreadLocals
None, every time, because pool threads clear their ThreadLocals between tasks
Whatever that pool thread last had: often none, sometimes a stale id from an earlier task
The logging call throws, because a ThreadLocal isn't thread-safe
quiz.why: The value lives on the worker thread. That thread was created long ago and is reused, so it holds nothing, or whatever an earlier task put there and never cleaned up. Nothing clears it between tasks unless your wrapper does.

quiz.q: Which number warns you first that a bounded `ThreadPoolExecutor` is falling behind, before it starts rejecting?
options: `getPoolSize()`
`getCompletedTaskCount()`
`getLargestPoolSize()`
`getQueue().size()` climbing, or the time tasks spend in the queue
quiz.why: A queue that keeps growing means arrivals outpace completions, and every queued task's wait grows with it. The pool size is fixed in a fixed pool, the completed count only ever rises, and the largest pool size is history. When the queue is full, rejections start.

quiz.q: The program's intake hands orders to `kitchenPool`, whose tasks submit to `billingPool`. The program is told to stop. In what order do you shut down?
options: Stop intake, shut down `kitchenPool` and wait for it, then shut down `billingPool` and wait for it
Shut down `billingPool`, then `kitchenPool`, then stop intake
Call `shutdownNow()` on both pools at once, to be quick
Stop intake, then shut down `billingPool` first, because it handles the money
quiz.why: Upstream first. While `kitchenPool` drains, its tasks still submit to `billingPool`, so `billingPool` must keep accepting work until then. Shutting it down first makes those submissions fail with `RejectedExecutionException`, and `shutdownNow` on both interrupts work that could have finished.

quiz.q: From "Inside ThreadPoolExecutor": a `ProductionPool` has 4 threads and a queue of 100, with the default `AbortPolicy`. 200 slow tasks arrive at once. How many are rejected?
quiz.why: Four tasks start the four threads, the next 100 fill the queue, and the core size equals the maximum, so the pool can't grow. The remaining 96 are rejected with `RejectedExecutionException`, which is what a bounded queue is for: the caller hears about the overload at once.

flashcards.front: How do you name pool threads on JDK 21+?
flashcards.back: Pass `Thread.ofPlatform().name("grill-", 0).factory()` to the executor. The threads are named grill-0, grill-1, ...
Only tasks run with `execute()`. With `submit()` the exception is stored in the Future, and nothing is printed.

flashcards.front: Why does a ThreadLocal value, such as a request id, disappear when you hand a task to a pool?
flashcards.back: The value belongs to the submitting thread, and the task runs on another thread. Capture it at submission and install it in the worker.

flashcards.front: Why must a context wrapper restore the worker's value in `finally`?
flashcards.back: Pool threads are reused. Whatever one task leaves behind becomes the next task's context.
Tasks in a bounded pool block waiting for other tasks queued in the same pool. Every thread waits, and the awaited tasks never start.

flashcards.front: Name two fixes for pool-induced deadlock.
flashcards.back: Compose instead of blocking (`supplyAsync(...).thenApply(...)`), or give each stage its own pool, so waits never point back into the same pool.

flashcards.front: In what order do you shut down chained pools?
flashcards.back: Stop intake, then shut down the upstream pool and wait, then the downstream one, all within one deadline.

terms.plain: The object a pool asks for new threads; it sets their names, daemon flag and exception handler.
A snapshot of every thread in a running JVM: its name, its state and the code it is running.
Code that runs when an exception escapes a thread's run method.
A variable with a separate value for each thread.
Mapped Diagnostic Context: a per-thread map of values, such as a request id, that SLF4J adds to log lines.
Copying thread-local state such as a request id from the submitting thread to the worker.
Every thread in a pool waits for a task that is queued in that same pool. Also called thread starvation deadlock.
Stopping intake, letting work in progress finish within a deadline, and recording what didn't.

explain_back.prompt: A friend's closing-time bill job works with 5 tables and hangs with 400, on a fixed pool of 20 threads. Explain what is happening and two ways to fix it.
explain_back.answer: Each table's task submits the fetch of its orders to the same pool and blocks on `get()`. With 400 tables, the first 20 tasks take every thread, and their fetches are queued behind the other 380 bill tasks. A fetch can only run on a free thread, and every thread is waiting for a fetch, so nothing ever finishes. The CPU is idle and nothing throws, because no lock is involved. One fix is to stop blocking inside the pool: start `supplyAsync(fetch, pool).thenApply(render)` for each table, so rendering is a callback and only the job's own thread waits at the end. Another is to run the fetches on a separate pool, so the bill threads wait on a pool that never waits back on them. Simplest of all, if the bill task only waits for the fetch, do the fetch inline.
